title: Email Collection via Local Email Access and Auto-Forwarding Behavior
shortTitle: Email Collection via Local Email Access and Auto-Forwardi...
summary: This strategy detects email collection through direct access to mailbox data on a user device and through server side auto-forwarding rules, which together cover the email collection technique. On the endpoint side the signal is a mail client or script reading local mailbox stores, such as a mail archive file or a local cache, especially by a process that is not the normal mail client. On the server side the signal is a new inbox rule that forwards or redirects mail to an external or unusual address, combined with the authentication events that preceded it. The telemetry needed is mailbox audit logging, identity sign-in records including legacy protocol access, and file access events on the local mail cache. It fails because forwarding rules and archive reads are everyday behaviour, so the rule must weigh the destination domain, the account's normal clients and the age of the rule.

beginner.definition: This detection covers two ways mail is taken. One is reading the mail files stored on a computer. The other is adding a rule in the mail service that quietly sends copies of new mail somewhere else. Both give an attacker your messages without needing your password again.
beginner.whyItMatters: Email holds password resets, contracts and private conversations. A forwarding rule keeps working after the attacker leaves and after a password change in some setups. Local mail files are easy to read and often not encrypted. Catching either case early limits what is taken and helps you warn the people involved.
howItWorks: The mail service records actions inside mailboxes, such as creating a rule or reading many messages.
The identity system records sign ins, including older mail protocols that do not support modern sign in checks.
The endpoint agent records which programs open the local mail cache or archive files.
The detection flags new forwarding rules that send mail outside your own domain.
It also flags unusual programs reading local mail files, or large reads by a normal one.
It links the two views by account so the analyst sees one story instead of two alerts.
beginner.example: Think of a shared letterbox in an apartment building. Anyone with a key can take the post. A second trick is to leave a note for the postman. The note says send all letters for flat three to another address. Both tricks take the same letters. This detection watches for the note as well as the key.
takeaways: Server side forwarding rules can outlive the session that created them.
Local mailbox files can be read by any program that can open the file, not just the mail client.
The forwarding destination and the account's normal mail clients are the fields that matter most.

objectives: Describe how mailbox forwarding rules and local mail file access both lead to email collection.
Identify the mailbox audit, sign-in and endpoint file access telemetry for each path.
Recognise signs of legacy mail protocol access that bypasses modern authentication controls.
Evaluate a new forwarding rule by destination domain and the account's normal client set.
Explain why reviewing rules is a standard step after any suspected mailbox compromise.
dataSources: Mail service mailbox audit logs recording rule creation and modification with the client address and user agent
Cloud identity sign-in logs showing legacy authentication protocols and the client application used
Endpoint detection and response file access events for local mail cache and archive file paths
Mail gateway or transport logs recording outbound messages with the sender, recipient domain and message size
Data loss prevention or cloud access security broker events for mail forwarded to personal or external domains
logic: The pattern is mailbox data leaving through a channel the account has not used before. Correlate the mailbox audit event that creates or changes a rule with the sign-in event that preceded it, sharing the account, the client address and the user agent, then compare the forwarding destination domain with the domains the organisation normally exchanges mail with. For local access, correlate endpoint file access on mail store paths with the process image, and flag processes that are not the approved mail client. In the benign case the user creates a rule to a colleague or an internal folder, the client is the managed mail application, and the same account uses the same client every day. In the malicious case the rule forwards to an external domain, it is created from an unusual address or an older protocol, and a script host or archive tool reads the local mail files.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Mailbox Forwarding Rule to External Domain with Legacy Sign-In
# logsource:
#   product: m365
#   service: mailbox_audit
# detection:
#   selection_rule:
#     operation:
#       - 'New-InboxRule'
#       - 'Set-InboxRule'
#     parameters|contains: 'ForwardTo'
#   filter_internal:
#     parameters|contains: '@example[.]com'
#   selection_auth:
#     operation: 'UserLoggedIn'
#     client_app|contains: 'legacy'
#   condition: selection_rule and not filter_internal and selection_auth
# level: high
falsePositives: Employees who forward work mail to a personal account so they can read it on a phone
Executive assistants who create forwarding rules for a manager's mailbox with documented approval
Mail migration or archiving tools that create temporary rules while moving a mailbox between tenants
Users who open an old mail archive file with a backup or search tool to find an old message
tuningNotes: Build two lists before enabling the rule: the domains your organisation legitimately exchanges mail with, and the approved mail applications and their file paths. Filter the forwarding rule on destination domain and the absence of a matching change request, and scope the local file access part to endpoints that hold mail archives and are not used for backup work. Baseline the number of rules an average user holds and alert on accounts that jump well above it. Narrowing by domain means you will miss collection to a compromised partner domain, so pair the rule with volume anomaly checks on outbound mail and with alerts on rule changes made from unusual addresses.
